Monday. Pradeep coloured every hour of Wednesday in his calendar, nine to six, with no gap between blocks, not even for tea. He showed Rukmini at the next desk. "Fully planned," he said, and grinned.

Wednesday. The client call meant to end at ten went on till eleven-fifteen. The report block was gone, the email block was gone, and by noon every box after it sat in the wrong place. He looked at the red pile and closed the calendar. The afternoon became replies and coffee refills, and the report was not sent.

Friday. Rukmini stopped at his desk. "I waited for the report until Thursday evening." Pradeep opened the calendar to the empty Wednesday. "It was all planned," he said.

qa.q: Until what time did the client call run?
qa.a: The client call went on till eleven-fifteen.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he showed Rukmini his calendar?
qa.a: Pradeep was proud and pleased, since he grinned and said it was fully planned.

qa.q: What could Pradeep change so that one long call does not wreck the day?
qa.a: Pradeep could leave short gaps between blocks and keep one flexible slot for overruns, so a long call only nudges things instead of breaking them.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have been affected by the missed report?
qa.a: Rukmini waited until Thursday evening, so may have been frustrated or worried about follow-on work, without knowing what had gone wrong.

grounding: Shows an employee boxing every hour with no slack so that one overrunning call makes him drop the schedule and miss a report.

passage:
Mehak, you've blocked your whole week in that calendar app, hour by hour, no gaps. Let your Nilesh Chachu tell you about my first job.
I was twenty-four, at an insurance office in Pune. I read somewhere that successful people plan every hour. So on Sunday night I filled Monday: 9 to 10 emails, 10 to 11 reports, 11 to 12 client calls, all the way to 7. Not one empty minute. I felt like a machine.
Monday, 10.15, my manager called me in for a "quick chat". It lasted fifty minutes. Now my reports ran into client calls. Client calls ran into lunch. By noon I was an hour behind on everything and the whole plan was useless.
I tore up the sheet and just reacted to whatever came, for the rest of the week.
The plan wasn't wrong, beta. It just had no breathing space.

qa.q: How long did the manager's quick chat last?
How did Nilesh feel by noon on Monday?
qa.a: Nilesh felt overwhelmed and defeated, an hour behind on everything with a plan that had become useless.

qa.q: When the chat ran long, what could Nilesh have done instead of tearing up the sheet, and why?
qa.a: He could have moved one block to later in the week and kept the rest, since a plan with some gaps can absorb one overrun.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's manager have seen the fifty-minute chat?
qa.a: The manager probably thought it was a normal quick chat and had no idea it wrecked Nilesh's tightly packed day.

grounding: It shows a young employee boxing every hour of his day with no gaps, so one long call pushes everything back and he abandons the schedule by noon.

passage:
The metro was delayed by twenty minutes that Tuesday, and Kiran's day was already broken before he reached the office. He had planned it like a train timetable: 9.00 stand-up, 9.15 to 10.30 budget sheet, 10.30 to 11.30 vendor call, 11.30 to 1.00 slides, lunch at 1.00 sharp. No gaps. Every minute used.
He walked in at 9.20, missed the stand-up and started the budget sheet late. At 10.30 the vendor rang on time, so the sheet stayed half done. The call ran long. The slides started at noon.
His colleague Kalyani passed his desk at 12.15. "Lunch?"
"I'm an hour behind," Kiran snapped. "My whole day's gone."
By one he had closed the calendar and was just answering whichever message pinged loudest. The schedule he'd spent Sunday evening making lay abandoned in a tab.

qa.q: How long was the metro delayed?
qa.a: The metro was delayed by twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when he snapped at Kalyani?
qa.a: He was stressed and irritable, feeling his whole day was ruined after falling an hour behind.

qa.q: What would you change first in Kiran's timetable?
qa.a: Add small gaps between blocks, like fifteen minutes after each call, so one delay doesn't push every task back.

qa.q: How might Kalyani experience Kiran's snapping?
qa.a: Kalyani may feel taken aback and a bit hurt, since she only asked about lunch.

grounding: It shows a young employee who packs every minute with no gaps, so one delay pushes everything back and he abandons the schedule by noon.
